claims.text: AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock is cobalt-free.
AlCrFeNiSi powder is typically processed by LPBF with a room-temperature build environment.
Room-temperature LPBF of AlCrFeNiSi produces rapid cooling and significant thermal gradients.
Room-temperature LPBF of AlCrFeNiSi produces dendritic solidification with compositional inhomogeneities.
Room-temperature LPBF of AlCrFeNiSi causes residual-stress accumulation and defect formation.
The LPBF build platform and powder bed should be maintained at approximately 500–600 °C during fabrication.
Preheating the LPBF build environment and substrate to 500–600 °C reduces thermal gradients during AlCrFeNiSi processing.
Lower thermal gradients promote more uniform nucleation and grain growth.
Preheating produces a finer and more homogeneous AlCrFeNiSi microstructure.
Preheating reduces dendritic segregation in LPBF-fabricated AlCrFeNiSi.
Elevating the substrate and ambient temperature reduces the solidification cooling rate.
The reduced cooling rate mitigates thermal shock and limits compositional and microstructural inhomogeneities.
Preheating reduces residual stress in LPBF-fabricated AlCrFeNiSi.
Preheating lowers defect density in LPBF-fabricated AlCrFeNiSi.
Preheated builds are predicted to have approximately 30% lower residual stress than room-temperature LPBF builds.
Preheating is predicted to increase the ductility of LPBF-fabricated AlCrFeNiSi.
Preheating is predicted to increase the toughness of LPBF-fabricated AlCrFeNiSi.
The expected mechanical improvements result from a more uniform, refined grain structure.
The hypothesis applies only when preheating to 500–600 °C does not induce oxidation or phase instability in AlCrFeNiSi.
Preliminary evidence from similar alloy systems supports thermal management through preheating.

contradictions.description: The intervention alternately requires heating the build environment, substrate, build platform, and powder bed, but the falsification experiment explicitly controls only build-platform temperature. The tested intervention therefore may not match the full hypothesized intervention.
